title: The energy bill of ultra events
goal: Explain how much energy ultramarathons, Ironman and multi-day bike races cost, how little of it athletes eat, and where the missing energy comes from.

steps.title: How big is the bill?
steps.text:
Ultra-endurance means events of many hours or days: ultramarathons (any run longer than 42.2 km), Ironman triathlon and multi-day bike races. The energy bill is huge.

- **Running** costs about 200–300 kJ per km, mostly depending on body mass. A 70 kg runner covering 161 km at 6.5 km·h⁻¹ uses about 41,400 kJ (9,891 kcal) in about 25 h [[c:ud-run-cost]].
- **Ironman** (3.8 km swim, 180 km ride, 42.2 km run): about 42,000 kJ (10,036 kcal) in men and 35,900 kJ (8,570 kcal) in women [[c:ud-ironman-ee]].
- **Race Across America**, a non-stop bike race across the USA: a four-rider relay team used on average 26,879 kJ (6,420 kcal) per rider per day for more than six days, measured with [doubly labelled water](g:doubly-labelled-water) [[c:ud-raam-ee]].

claims.text: Running costs about 200–300 kJ per km; a 70 kg runner doing 161 km at 6.5 km·h⁻¹ would use about 9,891 kcal in about 25 h.

evidence.quote: Second, a 50 kg athlete undertaking a 100 mile (161 km) ultra-marathon at an average pace of 6.5 km·h− 1 may expend ~ 6922 Kcal in ~ 25 h, whereas at the same pace, a 70 kg athlete would likely expend ~ 9891 Kcal (range of 277–395 Kcal·h− 1).
These values are similar to the estimated energy expenditures of 200–300 kJ·km− 1 (47.8–71.7 Kcal·km− 1) reported elsewhere

claims.text: In an Ironman, estimated energy expenditure was about 10,036 kcal in men and 8,570 kcal in women.

evidence.quote: Total EE (10,036 +/- 931 and 8,570 +/- 1,014 kcal) was significantly greater than total EI (3,940 +/- 868 and 3,115 +/- 914 kcal, p <.001) for males and females, respectively

claims.text: A four-rider Race Across America relay team used on average 6,420 kcal (26,879 kJ) per day, measured with doubly labelled water.

evidence.quote: Total mean energy expenditure was found to be 43,401 kcals (181,711 kJ) with a mean daily energy expenditure of 6,420 kcals (26,879 kJ).

steps.title: Estimating a race's energy cost
steps.problem: Estimate the energy used by (1) a 70 kg runner covering 100 km and (2) a cyclist riding 8 h at an average 200 W. Take the cost of running as 4.1 kJ·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹ and gross efficiency as 20%.
steps: Running: energy = mass × distance × cost per kg per km = 70 × 100 × 4.1 = 28,700 kJ (about 6,860 kcal).
Cycling, step 1, the work on the pedals: 200 W × 8 h × 3,600 s·h⁻¹ = 5,760,000 J = 5,760 kJ. This is the kJ number your power meter shows.
Cycling, step 2: only about 20% of the energy used becomes work, so energy used = work ÷ 0.20 = 5,760 ÷ 0.20 = 28,800 kJ (about 6,880 kcal).

Both are estimates to about ±10%: running cost differs between runners, and one point of gross efficiency changes the cycling figure by about 5%. Tiller's running figure (about 3.7 kJ·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹ in the example on the card) is a little lower than the 4.1 used here.

steps.title: What athletes actually eat
steps.text:
Field studies count food at aid stations or ask athletes afterwards ([dietary recall](g:dietary-recall)). The finding is the same everywhere: athletes eat only about a third to a half of what they use, 36–53% in ultra-endurance races [[c:ud-intake-share]].

In an Ironman, men ate about 16,500 kJ (3,940 kcal) against about 42,000 kJ used, leaving a gap of about 25,500 kJ [[c:ud-ironman-ei]]. Race Across America riders did better, eating 20,591 kJ (4,918 kcal) a day, but still ended with a total [energy deficit](g:energy-deficit) of 58,104 kJ (13,878 kcal) [[c:ud-raam-deficit]].

Why the gap? Gut trouble, food that becomes hard to face, aid stations far apart, the weight of what you carry and lack of sleep all get in the way [[c:ud-barriers]].

claims.text: Ultra-endurance athletes eat about 36–53% of the energy they use while racing; race completion goes with higher energy and fluid intake.

evidence.quote: Indeed, while race completion has been positively correlated with energy and fluid intake [14, 15], the calories consumed by some ultra-endurance athletes is reported to be between 36 and 53% of their racing energy expenditure

claims.text: In an Ironman, men ate about 3,940 kcal and women about 3,115 kcal, far less than they used.

evidence.quote: Total EE (10,036 +/- 931 and 8,570 +/- 1,014 kcal) was significantly greater than total EI (3,940 +/- 868 and 3,115 +/- 914 kcal, p <.001) for males and females, respectively

claims.text: Race Across America riders ate 4,918 kcal (20,591 kJ) a day and ended with a total energy deficit of 13,878 kcal (58,104 kJ).

evidence.quote: Total mean energy intake from all food and drink consumed was calculated at 29,506 kcals (123,536 kJ) with a mean daily energy intake of 4 918 kcals (20,591 kJ). This resulted in a total mean energy deficit of 13,878 kcals (58,104 kJ)

claims.text: Barriers to eating in ultras include gut distress, irregular checkpoints, pack weight, changing palatability, and sleep deprivation and environmental extremes that affect appetite.

evidence.quote: a high prevalence of athlete gastrointestinal (GI) distress; inconsistent food/fluid timing and rationing at checkpoints; the need to minimize pack-weight in self-sufficient races; placebo effects and confirmation bias from prior race experiences; the changes in food/fluid palatability associated with prolonged endurance exercise; sleep deprivation and extremes of temperature/altitude which are known to influence appetite

steps.title: Where the missing energy comes from
steps.text:
An energy deficit is paid from body stores. [Glycogen](g:glycogen) is small: about 400 g in muscle and 80–100 g in the liver, roughly 8,000–8,500 kJ (about 2,000 kcal) in all. Fat is vast: even a lean athlete carries about 125,000 kJ (over 30,000 kcal).

Ultras are done at low intensity, and as glycogen falls the body burns more fat: typically 0.2–0.5 g of fat per minute, and the slow pace of ultras allows high fat use [[c:ud-fat-shift]]. So fat covers most of the gap, and [RER](g:rer) drifts down over the hours.

But glycogen can still run out if the pace is too high or eating is poor [[c:ud-glycogen-risk]]. In Ironman racing, athletes who ate more carbohydrate per hour tended to finish faster [[c:ud-cho-faster]]. Fat covers the bulk; carbohydrate holds the pace.

claims.text: As muscle glycogen falls, fat oxidation rises (typically 0.2–0.5 g·min⁻¹), and the long durations and slow relative speeds of ultras allow high fat oxidation.

evidence.quote: As muscle glycogen diminishes, there is a compensatory increase in fat oxidation, with rates of 0.2–0.5 g·min− 1 typically observed during endurance exercise
The prolonged durations and slower relative running speeds that characterize ultra-marathon appear, therefore, to permit increased rates of fat oxidation for adenosine triphosphate (ATP) re-synthesis

claims.text: Glycogen can still run out in an ultra if the work rate is too high or nutrition is poorly managed.

evidence.quote: However, there is still a risk of glycogen depletion during ultra-marathon if work rate is too high, or if nutrition is poorly managed.

claims.text: In Ironman races, higher carbohydrate intake per hour went with faster finishing times (observational).

evidence.quote: Total CHO intake rates were positively correlated with nausea and flatulence but were negatively correlated with finishing time during both IM (r = -0.55 and r = -0.48, P < 0.001).
Finishing time was inversely related to carbohydrate (CHO) intake (g x kg(-1) x h(-1)) during the marathon run for males (r = -.75,p <.05), and not females

steps.title: Sleep loss, appetite and eating anyway
steps.text:
In races longer than 24 h and in multi-day events, sleep is cut short, and sleep loss is one of the things known to change appetite.

In a lab study of 23 young adults, one night without sleep changed how the brain responded to food and raised the desire for high-calorie foods [[c:ud-sleep-desire]]. That might even help a depleted rider eat. But it's one night, in people at rest, not athletes: nobody has shown how sleep loss changes eating during a race.

What the ISSN does advise: when nausea or low appetite hits, slow down and eat less for a while if you must, but don't stay below about 840 kJ (200 kcal) per hour for long in longer races. Some stubbornness about eating is part of the job [[c:ud-eat-anyway]].

claims.text: One night of sleep deprivation raised the desire for high-calorie foods and changed brain responses to food in healthy young adults.

evidence.quote: Moreover, this bi-directional change in the profile of brain activity is further associated with a significant increase in the desire for weight-gain promoting high-calorie foods following sleep deprivation, the extent of which is predicted by the subjective severity of sleep loss across participants.

claims.text: When symptoms appear, runners can slow down and eat less, but persistent intakes below 200 kcal·h⁻¹ should be avoided in longer races; some perseverance with feeding may be needed.

evidence.quote: When symptoms manifest, runners can slow their pace and decrease their calorie intake, although persistent intakes of < 200 Kcal·h− 1 should be avoided in longer races.

However, persistent calorie intakes of < 200 Kcal·h− 1 are not recommended, and when nausea precludes this rate of intake, a degree of perseverance/stubbornness with respect to feeding (within tolerance levels) may be required.

points: Ultra events cost tens of thousands of kJ: about 42,000 kJ (10,000 kcal) for an Ironman, about 27,000 kJ (6,400 kcal) a day in a multi-day bike race.
Estimate the bill from parts: running ≈ mass × km × about 4.1 kJ; cycling = power-meter kJ ÷ gross efficiency (about 0.20).
Athletes eat only about 36–53% of what they use in ultra races; gut trouble, food fatigue, logistics and sleep loss get in the way.
Fat stores cover most of the deficit at ultra intensities, but glycogen can still run out, and more carbohydrate per hour went with faster Ironman times.
Sleep loss shifts appetite toward high-calorie food in lab studies; in races, keep eating at least about 840 kJ (200 kcal) per hour.

variants.stem: A 55 kg runner covers a 161 km ultramarathon. Taking the cost of running as 4.1 kJ·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹, about how much energy does she use?

options.text: About 36,300 kJ
About 8,860 kJ
options.why: This is 55 × 161 only: it leaves out the 4.1 kJ each kg costs per km.

options.text: About 660 kJ
options.why: This is 161 × 4.1 only: it leaves out body mass, and the cost is per kg.

options.text: About 145,200 kJ
options.why: This multiplies the answer by 4 again, as if converting kcal to kJ. The result is already in kJ.

variants.solution: Energy = mass × distance × cost = 55 kg × 161 km × 4.1 kJ·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹ = 36,306 kJ ≈ 36,300 kJ (about 8,680 kcal).

variants.stem: A cyclist rides a 10 h ultra-distance event at an average 180 W with a gross efficiency of 20%. About how much energy does she use?

options.text: About 32,400 kJ
About 6,480 kJ
options.why: That's the work on the pedals (the power-meter kJ). It forgets that only about 20% of the energy used becomes work.

options.text: About 1,300 kJ
options.why: This multiplies the work by 0.20 instead of dividing by it.

options.text: About 108 kJ
options.why: This uses minutes (600) instead of seconds (36,000) for the time, and leaves out efficiency.

variants.stem: In an Ironman, a triathlete rides the 180 km bike leg in 5.5 h at an average 160 W, with a gross efficiency of 20%. About how much energy does the bike leg use?

options.text: About 15,840 kJ
About 3,170 kJ
options.why: That's the work on the pedals. It forgets that only about 20% of the energy used becomes work.

options.text: About 630 kJ
options.why: This multiplies the work by 0.20 instead of dividing by it.

options.text: About 53 kJ
options.why: This uses minutes (330) instead of seconds (19,800), and leaves out efficiency.

variants.stem: In field studies of ultra-endurance races, about what share of the energy they use do athletes eat during the race?

options.text: About 36–53%
options.why: Right: intake covers roughly a third to a half of race energy use.

options.text: About 90–100%
options.why: Nobody keeps pace with expenditure that high for that long; the gut and logistics don't allow it.

options.text: Under 10%
options.why: Too low: athletes do eat a lot, just not enough. Even the Ironman men ate about 16,500 kJ.

options.text: More than they use
options.why: Race studies show a deficit, not a surplus; surplus intake belongs to the days before a race.

variants.stem: A 100-mile trail runner uses about 40,000 kJ but eats about 15,000 kJ. What mainly explains the gap?

options.text: Gut distress, food fatigue, sparse aid stations and pack weight limit intake
options.why: Right: these practical and gut barriers stop athletes from eating what they use.

options.text: Eating more would stop the body from burning fat during the race
options.why: Eating carbohydrate lowers fat use somewhat, but the body still burns plenty of fat; that isn't why intake is low.

options.text: The body needs no food in a race because fat covers every need
options.why: Glycogen can still run out, and finishing goes with eating more; food clearly matters.

options.text: Expenditure estimates are wrong, so there is no real gap
options.why: The estimates have error (about ±10%), but not enough to close a gap of more than half.

variants.stem: Race Across America riders used 26,879 kJ a day and ate 20,591 kJ a day. What share of their daily use did they eat?

options.text: About 77%
About 131%
options.why: This divides use by intake (26,879 ÷ 20,591), the wrong way round.

options.text: About 23%
options.why: That's the share they did not cover: the deficit, (26,879 − 20,591) ÷ 26,879.

options.text: About 39%
options.why: That's the Ironman men's figure, not a calculation from these numbers.

variants.solution: Share eaten = intake ÷ expenditure = 20,591 ÷ 26,879 = 0.766 ≈ 77%. Daily deficit = 26,879 − 20,591 = 6,288 kJ (about 1,500 kcal).

variants.stem: In an Ironman, women used about 35,860 kJ and ate about 13,030 kJ. What share of their use did they eat?

options.text: About 36%
About 275%
options.why: This divides use by intake (35,860 ÷ 13,030), the wrong way round.

options.text: About 64%
options.why: That's the share they did not cover: the deficit, (35,860 − 13,030) ÷ 35,860.

options.text: About 77%
options.why: That's the Race Across America figure, not a calculation from these numbers.

variants.solution: Share eaten = intake ÷ expenditure = 13,030 ÷ 35,860 = 0.363 ≈ 36%. Deficit = 35,860 − 13,030 = 22,830 kJ (about 5,460 kcal).

variants.stem: An Ironman study (18 athletes) estimated energy use from lab heart rate–VO₂ equations and intake from dietary recall at 7 points on the course. What most limits trust in the size of the deficit it found?

options.text: Heart rate drifts up over hours at the same VO₂, and recall can misjudge intake
options.why: Right: [cardiovascular drift](g:cardiovascular-drift) makes heart-rate equations overestimate late-race energy use, and recall errors blur intake. The deficit is real, but its exact size is uncertain.

options.text: Men and women were mixed, so neither group's data can be read
options.why: They were reported separately (about 42,000 vs 35,900 kJ used), and the deficit was similar in both.

options.text: Doubly labelled water would have given minute-by-minute values
options.why: Doubly labelled water gives an average over days; it suits multi-day events, not minute-by-minute values.

options.text: An Ironman is too short to cause any real energy deficit
options.why: Even with generous error bars, using about 42,000 kJ and eating about 16,500 kJ leaves a large deficit.

variants.stem: Roughly how much energy does the body store as glycogen, in muscle and liver together?

options.why: Right: about 400 g in muscle plus 80–100 g in the liver, at about 17 kJ per gram.

options.text: About 125,000 kJ
options.why: That's the fat stored by a lean athlete, about 15 times more than glycogen.

options.text: About 800 kJ
options.why: Ten times too small: that's about 50 g of carbohydrate, about two gels.

options.text: About 42,000 kJ
options.why: That's the energy used in a whole Ironman; glycogen alone could never cover it.

variants.stem: A runner's RER is 0.90 in hour 1 of a 24 h race and 0.78 in hour 18 at a similar easy pace. Best explanation?

options.text: Glycogen has fallen and fat now supplies a bigger share
options.why: Right: as glycogen falls, fat oxidation rises, and RER moves toward 0.7.

options.text: Her running economy improved, so she uses less energy
options.why: RER shows the fuel mix, not how much energy is used.

options.text: She is now burning mainly protein
options.why: Protein's RQ is about 0.8, but it only ever supplies a small share; the fall reflects more fat.

options.text: She is working harder than in hour 1
options.why: Harder work raises RER toward 1.0 as carbohydrate use rises; this went the other way.

variants.stem: On day 3 of a multi-day bike race, a rider's RER at his usual easy pace is 0.79, against 0.88 on day 1. Best explanation?

options.text: Lower glycogen, so fat supplies a bigger share
options.why: Right: with glycogen down after days of deficit, fat oxidation rises and RER falls toward 0.7.

options.text: His gross efficiency has risen sharply
options.why: RER reflects the fuel mix, not efficiency.

options.text: He is now burning mainly protein
options.why: Protein supplies only a small share; an RER near 0.8 here mostly reflects more fat.

options.text: He is riding harder than on day 1
options.why: Harder riding raises RER; this fell.

variants.stem: A triathlete says: "I carry 125,000 kJ of fat, so in an Ironman I don't need carbohydrate." Best reply?

options.text: Fat covers most of the deficit, but glycogen can still run out at race pace
options.why: Right: fat is the big store, but glycogen sets how hard you can go, and more carbohydrate per hour went with faster Ironman times.

options.text: True: at Ironman intensity fat supplies all the energy
options.why: At Ironman pace carbohydrate still supplies a large share; fat alone can't hold that intensity.

options.text: False: fat can only be burned at rest, not in exercise
options.why: Fat is burned during exercise, typically 0.2–0.5 g per minute, more as glycogen falls.

options.text: False: fat stores are too small to matter in an Ironman
options.why: Fat stores are about 15 times larger than glycogen: they are the main reserve.

variants.stem: On day 4 of a multi-day bike race, after very little sleep, a rider craves crisps and chocolate. What does the evidence say?

options.text: Sleep loss raised the desire for high-calorie food in a lab study; racing effects are unknown
options.why: Right: one night without sleep did this in 23 young adults at rest; it hasn't been shown in racing athletes.

options.text: Sleep loss always kills appetite, so the cravings must mean low blood sugar
options.why: The lab study found the opposite: more desire for high-calorie food after sleep loss.

options.text: Race Across America studies proved that sleep loss doubles intake
options.why: No race study has shown this; the evidence is one lab study of non-athletes.

options.text: The cravings mean he is eating too much and should cut back
options.why: Multi-day riders run large deficits; the cravings don't signal a surplus.

variants.stem: In hour 15 of a 100-mile run, a runner feels sick and has eaten only about 400 kJ an hour for the last 3 hours. What fits the ISSN advice?

options.text: Slow a little and keep taking small amounts, working back to at least about 840 kJ an hour
options.why: Right: slowing and easing intake is fine for a while, but intakes below about 840 kJ (200 kcal) per hour shouldn't persist.

options.text: Stop eating until the nausea has completely gone, however long it takes
options.why: Long stretches with almost no intake risk running out of carbohydrate and not finishing.

options.text: Eat a big meal at once to make up the missing 3 hours
options.why: A large load on an upset gut is likely to make the nausea worse; small, frequent amounts are kinder.

options.text: Switch to plain water only until the finish
options.why: That gives no energy for the rest of the race, and lots of plain water risks low blood sodium.
